_about: Materials reference round (parity batch B4): temper and heat-tint colours, heat treatment, galvanic series, machining plastics, metal identification. Every value records what one free publisher prints (verbatim or close transcription in 'v'), with the source key. Temperatures are stored in degC as printed or as converted from the printed degF (the printed text is kept in 'v'). Copies of one source share a 'family' and count once. Explanatory text (terms, notes, tips) is BenchMate's own wording; the sources listed against it use the term or say the same thing. No handbook table (Machinery's Handbook or similar) was used.

temper_carbon._note: Colour keys are ours; each publisher's own colour name is kept. Matched by name: 'golden yellow' and 'dark yellow' as dark yellow, 'brown dappled with purple' and 'red brown' as brown-purple, 'bright blue' and 'Wedgewood blue' as bright blue, 'pale blue' and 'light blue' as light blue.

tint_stainless._note: Heated in air. The British Stainless Steel Association chart as reproduced by Wikipedia; Heat Treat Today gives the same order of colours by oxide thickness but its temperature chart is an image.

colour_factors: A longer soak gives a deeper colour at the same temperature, so a colour reached slowly shows a lower temperature than the chart.
Colours form by oxidation; oxygen and water vapour in the furnace gas (air or a leak) colour the surface, a clean inert or vacuum atmosphere does not.
Charts differ by alloy: stainless steels colour at higher temperatures than plain carbon steel, and higher chromium slows the tint.
A rougher or dirty surface oxidises faster and shows deeper colours; clean, bright metal is needed to read a colour at all.
titanium_note: Titanium heat-tint colours are not given: the sources read give titanium weld colour only as a sign of contamination (judged against the weld specification, for example AWS D17.1), not as a temperature, and no two free publishers print a titanium temperature chart.

terms.own: Heating steel to a set temperature, holding it and cooling it very slowly (often in the furnace) so it is as soft and machinable as it gets. Tool steels are supplied 'soft annealed'.
A long soak just below or around the lower critical temperature that turns the carbides into small balls; the softest condition for cold forming and machining high-carbon steels.
Heating above the hardening range and cooling in still air. Refines the grain and evens out the structure after forging or rolling; harder than annealed, softer than hardened.

Heating well below the hardening range (for hardened steel, below the last tempering temperature) and cooling slowly, to release stresses from rough machining, welding or straightening without changing hardness much. Tool makers advise it between roughing and finishing.

Heating the steel into its hardening range (austenitising), soaking it until it is heated through, then cooling it fast enough (the quench) to form hard martensite. The quench medium (water, oil, polymer, air, gas) is set by the grade.

Water is the most severe quench, then polymer solutions and oil; air-hardening steels (A2, D2, H13, S7) harden in still or forced air or gas, which distorts less. A martempering (hot bath) quench stops just above the martensite start temperature to even out the part before it cools.

Reheating hardened steel to a temperature below the hardening range, holding it and cooling it. It trades some hardness for toughness and must follow the quench at once (tool makers say when the part reaches about 50-70 °C). Tool steels are usually tempered twice or more.
Quenching into a hot salt bath or fluidised bed held just above the martensite start, equalising, then cooling in air. Less distortion and cracking than a direct quench.
Adding carbon to the surface of a low-carbon steel at high temperature, then hardening, so a hard skin sits on a tough core. Used for gears, pins and wear parts made of grades such as 8620.

Diffusing nitrogen into the surface at a relatively low temperature (around 500 °C) for many hours. No quench, so very little distortion; gives a thin, very hard case on nitriding steels, 4140, 4340, H13 and similar.

Heating only the surface quickly (with an induction coil or a flame) and quenching it, leaving the core as it was. Needs a steel with enough carbon (medium-carbon and alloy steels such as 1045, 4140, 4340), usually followed by a low temper.

For precipitation-hardening stainless steels such as 17-4PH: the bar is supplied solution treated (condition A); a single ageing at a lower temperature then raises strength. The condition name is the ageing temperature in °F (H900 = 900 °F). Ageing shrinks the part slightly.

galv_sea._note: Seawater at 77 °F (25 °C), potential in volts against a silver/silver-chloride reference, as printed in millivolts by Gerr. Most negative = most anodic (corrodes first).

GERR.text: keep the voltage difference between two metals in direct contact in seawater below 0.20 V; above that, insulate them from each other or protect them with anodes

galv_order._note: Wikipedia's order, most noble first, for stagnant (low-oxygen) seawater. 'k' links an entry to a row of the Gerr table where the metal is the same; entries without k have no counterpart.

anodic_index._note: Anodic index in volts (gold = 0). A higher index is more anodic. Not a seawater measurement: a design table for choosing compatible metals and finishes.

ENSINGER_MG.v: TECAMID 6 PA6 3 h to 194°F 3 h to 320°F

notes: Takes up water and swells (Ensinger: about 0.5 % in size per 3 % moisture): leave allowance on close fits and store stock dry.

ENSINGER_MG.v: TECAPEEK PEEK 3 h to 250°F 4 h to 430°F

notes: Machines well with short chips; carbide tools (MCAM lists carbide only). Filled grades (glass, carbon) are abrasive: carbide or diamond tools and lower speeds.
Keep heat input low to limit post-shrinkage; anneal between roughing and finishing for tight tolerances.

UHMWPE.name: UHMW-PE
notes: Very soft and tough: needs sharp tools and burrs readily (Ensinger says this of soft, tough plastics such as PE and PTFE). Large thermal expansion: measure parts at room temperature.

PTFE.name: PTFE (virgin)
notes: Soft, creeps under clamping force and smears: very sharp tools, light clamping, and expect fuzz and burrs that need deburring.
MCAM's PTFE rows are for its filled Fluorosint grades and are not used for virgin PTFE.

PC.name: Polycarbonate (PC)

ENSINGER_MG.v: TECANAT PC 3 h to 175°F 3 h to 265°F

notes: Amorphous: stress-cracks with oils, greases and many cutting fluids. Machine dry or with a water-based fluid and wash parts afterwards (MCAM: isopropyl alcohol, then water).
Sharp tools, light feeds, round inside corners.

PMMA.name: Acrylic (PMMA, cast)
notes: Brittle and notch sensitive: Boedeker prints a small rake (0-4°); support thin parts. Amorphous like PC, so avoid mineral-oil coolants.

PVC.name: PVC (rigid, type I)
notes: Softens at a low temperature: keep the cut cool with air. Overheated PVC gives off corrosive fumes, so never let it burn; keep chips off machine slides.

PP.name: Polypropylene (PP)
notes: Soft and tough like PE: sharp tools, burrs readily, and large thermal expansion.

ABS.name: ABS
notes: Amorphous and tough; a large positive rake is printed for it. Avoid oily coolants, as with other amorphous plastics.

PEI.name: PEI (Ultem 1000 type, unfilled)
notes: Amorphous and stiff; stress-cracks with some fluids like PC, so machine dry or with a water-based fluid. Carbide tools.

general: Plastics conduct heat poorly and expand up to about ten times as much as metals: keep heat out of the part with sharp, positive tools and enough feed to cut chips rather than rub.
Coolant is mostly not needed: air blast or a water-based fluid. Mineral-oil fluids can stress-crack amorphous plastics (PC, PMMA, PEI, PSU, ABS).
For tight tolerances, rough, let the part rest (MCAM: 24 hours) or anneal it, then finish. Diameters tend to grow after machining, so aim low in the tolerance (MCAM).
Measure at room temperature: a part measured warm from the machine is oversize by its expansion.
Drilling generates the most heat: peck, clear chips, and use a lower speed than turning (MCAM: 25-100 m/min, 90-120° point).
Test on scrap first; grades and fillers change the right numbers.

spark._note: Stream lengths are for the same wheel and pressure in the Navy manual and only compare metals with each other.
rows: straw near the wheel, brighter red at the end
few forked sparklers near the end
red near the wheel, straw further out
straw near the wheel, white at the end
no sparklers (the two cannot be told apart this way)

tests: Touch the metal lightly to a grinding wheel and compare the stream with known samples on the same wheel: more carbon gives more, smaller bursts (sparklers). Wear eye protection and keep clear of others.
Iron-based (ferrous) metals are normally attracted by a magnet and nonferrous metals are not; some stainless steels are not magnetic, so the test is not fully reliable.

Ferritic and martensitic stainless (400 series) are attracted by a magnet, annealed austenitic stainless (300 series) is not, and cold-worked 300 series can be slightly magnetic: a magnet alone never proves a grade.

Cut a small chip with a sharp cold chisel and compare with known samples: the size and edges of the chip, its grain, and how easily it cuts all help to tell metals apart (the Navy manual tabulates them).
A file bites easily into soft (annealed) steel, harder into tool steel, and skates over hardened steel; it gives a rough idea of hardness only. Use a proper hardness tester for numbers.
Colour, surface (mill scale, cast skin, machined), and weight for size separate aluminium, titanium, copper alloys and steel quickly.
For a grade that matters, trust the mill certificate, a positive material identification (XRF or OES) analysis, or a lab: the tests above only sort metals into families.
